title: Merge Sorted Array
description:
You are given two arrays that are already sorted in non-decreasing order. Combine them into one array that is also sorted in non-decreasing order.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: two integers `m` and `n`, the length of the first array and the length of the second array.
- Line 2: the `m` integers of the first array (an empty line when `m` is 0).
- Line 3: the `n` integers of the second array (an empty line when `n` is 0).

Output (stdout):

- One line with all `m + n` integers in sorted order, separated by single spaces.
constraints:
- `0 <= m, n <= 200`
- `1 <= m + n <= 400`
- `-1000 <= each value <= 1000`
- Both input arrays are already sorted in non-decreasing order.

title: Remove Element
description:
Remove every copy of a given value from an array, keeping the surviving elements in their original relative order.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the length of the array.
- Line 2: the `n` integers of the array.
- Line 3: the integer `val` to remove.

Output (stdout):

- Line 1: `k`, the number of elements that are not equal to `val`.
- Line 2: the `k` surviving elements in their original order, separated by single spaces. Print this line only when `k` is greater than 0.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
description:
An array is sorted in non-decreasing order. Keep only one copy of each distinct value, preserving the sorted order.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the length of the array.
- Line 2: the `n` sorted integers of the array.

Output (stdout):

- Line 1: `k`, the number of distinct values.
- Line 2: those `k` values in sorted order, separated by single spaces.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 300`
- `-100 <= each value <= 100`
- The array is already sorted in non-decreasing order.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
description:
An array is sorted in non-decreasing order. Keep at most two copies of each distinct value, preserving the sorted order.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the length of the array.
- Line 2: the `n` sorted integers of the array.

Output (stdout):

- Line 1: `k`, the number of elements that remain.
- Line 2: those `k` elements in sorted order, separated by single spaces.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 300`
- `-10000 <= each value <= 10000`
- The array is already sorted in non-decreasing order.

title: Majority Element
topics: Array, Hash Table, Divide and Conquer, Counting
description:
One value in the array occurs more than `n / 2` times. Report that value.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the length of the array.
- Line 2: the `n` integers of the array.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the majority value.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 500`
- `-1000 <= each value <= 1000`
- A majority value always exists, so it occurs more than `n / 2` times.

title: Rotate Array
description:
Shift every element of an array `k` positions to the right. Elements pushed past the end wrap around to the front.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: two integers `n` and `k`, the length of the array and the number of right shifts. `k` can be larger than `n`.
- Line 2: the `n` integers of the array.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the rotated array, separated by single spaces.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
description:
You are given the price of one share on each of `n` consecutive days. Buy on one day and sell on a later day, at most once, and report the largest profit you can make. If no trade makes money, the profit is 0.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the number of days.
- Line 2: the `n` prices, one per day, in day order.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the largest profit.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
description:
You are given the price of one share on each of `n` consecutive days. You may buy and sell as often as you like, but you can hold at most one share at a time, and you must sell before buying again. Report the largest total profit.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the number of days.
- Line 2: the `n` prices, one per day, in day order.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the largest total profit.

title: Jump Game
description:
You start on the first cell of an array. The value in a cell is the largest number of cells you may move forward from there. Decide whether the last cell can be reached.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the length of the array.
- Line 2: the `n` jump lengths.

Output (stdout):

- One line holding `true` when the last cell is reachable, otherwise `false`, in lowercase.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
5
2 3 1 1 4
Output:
true
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
5
3 2 1 0 4
Output:
false
```
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 300`
- `0 <= each jump length <= 300`

title: Jump Game II
description:
You start on the first cell of an array. The value in a cell is the largest number of cells you may move forward from there, and the last cell is always reachable. Report the fewest jumps needed to land on the last cell.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the length of the array.
- Line 2: the `n` jump lengths.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the fewest number of jumps. It is 0 when `n` is 1.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 300`
- `0 <= each jump length <= 300`
- The last cell is always reachable from the first cell.

title: H-Index
description:
A researcher has `n` papers, and you are given how many times each paper was cited. The h-index is the largest value `h` such that at least `h` of the papers have `h` or more citations each. Report the h-index.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the number of papers.
- Line 2: the `n` citation counts, in any order.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the h-index.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 500`
- `0 <= each citation count <= 1000`

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
topics: Array, Hash Table, Math, Design, Randomized
description:
Build a collection of distinct integers that supports inserting a value, removing a value, and returning a uniformly random member, each in average constant time. Replay a list of operations on an initially empty collection.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `q`, the number of operations.
- Next `q` lines: one operation each, in one of these forms:
  - `insert x` - add `x` to the collection.
  - `remove x` - delete `x` from the collection.
  - `getRandom` - pick a uniformly random member.

Output (stdout):

- One line per operation:
  - `insert x` prints `true` when `x` was not present and was added, otherwise `false`.
  - `remove x` prints `true` when `x` was present and was deleted, otherwise `false`.
  - `getRandom` prints `true` when the picked value is a current member, and `none` when the collection is empty.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
5
insert 1
remove 2
insert 2
getRandom
remove 1
Output:
true
false
true
true
true
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
4
getRandom
insert 3
insert 3
getRandom
Output:
none
true
false
true
```
constraints:
- `1 <= q <= 200`
- `-1000 <= x <= 1000`
- Every operation name is exactly `insert`, `remove`, or `getRandom`.

6
insert -5
insert -5
remove -5
remove -5
getRandom
insert 0
testCases.output:
true
false
true
false
none
true

testCases.input:
7
insert 10
insert 20
insert 30
remove 20
getRandom
remove 30
remove 10
testCases.output:
true
true
true
true
true
true
true

title: Product of Array Except Self
description:
For each position of an array, compute the product of all the other elements.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the length of the array.
- Line 2: the `n` integers of the array.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the `n` products, in the same order as the input, separated by single spaces.
constraints:
- `2 <= n <= 300`
- `-30 <= each value <= 30`
- Every product fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

title: Gas Station
description:
There are `n` gas stations arranged in a circle. Station `i` gives you `gas[i]` units of fuel, and driving from station `i` to the next station burns `cost[i]` units. You start with an empty tank and must finish the whole loop without the tank ever going negative. Report a station you can start from.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the number of stations.
- Line 2: the `n` values of `gas`.
- Line 3: the `n` values of `cost`.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the index of a workable starting station, counting from 0. If several stations work, print the smallest such index. Print `-1` when no station works.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 300`
- `0 <= each gas value <= 1000`
- `0 <= each cost value <= 1000`

title: Candy
description:
Children stand in a row and each has a rating. Give every child at least one candy, and give a child strictly more candies than a neighbour whose rating is lower. Report the smallest total number of candies that satisfies both rules.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the number of children.
- Line 2: the `n` ratings, in row order.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the smallest total number of candies.

title: Trapping Rain Water
topics: Array, Two Pointers, Dynamic Programming, Stack
description:
Bars of width 1 stand side by side, and the array gives their heights. After rain, water settles in the dips between taller bars. Report how many units of water are held.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the number of bars.
- Line 2: the `n` bar heights, left to right.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the total units of trapped water.

title: Roman to Integer
description:
Roman numerals use the symbols `I`, `V`, `X`, `L`, `C`, `D`, and `M` for 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, and 1000. Symbols are normally written from largest to smallest and added up, but a smaller symbol placed directly before a larger one is subtracted instead, as in `IV` for 4 and `CM` for 900. Convert a roman numeral to its decimal value.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the roman numeral, in uppercase letters with no spaces.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the decimal value.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
LVIII
Output:
58
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
MCMXCIV
Output:
1994
```
constraints:
- The numeral is 1 to 15 characters long.
- It contains only the characters `I`, `V`, `X`, `L`, `C`, `D`, and `M`.
- It is a valid roman numeral for a value between 1 and 3999.

title: Integer to Roman
description:
Roman numerals use the symbols `I`, `V`, `X`, `L`, `C`, `D`, and `M` for 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, and 1000, plus the subtractive pairs `IV`, `IX`, `XL`, `XC`, `CD`, and `CM` for 4, 9, 40, 90, 400, and 900. Write a decimal number as the standard roman numeral, which always takes the largest symbol or pair that still fits, from left to right.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the decimal number.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the roman numeral, in uppercase letters with no spaces.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
3749
Output:
MMMDCCXLIX
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
1994
Output:
MCMXCIV
```

title: Length of Last Word
description:
A line holds words made of letters, separated by one or more spaces. Report how many letters the last word has.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the sentence. It may begin with spaces and may use runs of several spaces between words.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the length of the last word.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
Hello World
Output:
5
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
   fly me   to   the moon
Output:
4
```
constraints:
- The line is 1 to 200 characters long.
- It contains only English letters and spaces.
- It holds at least one word.

title: Longest Common Prefix
description:
Find the longest run of characters that starts every one of the given words.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `n`, the number of words.
- Next `n` lines: one word each.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the longest common prefix, or `none` when the words share no starting character.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
3
flower
flow
flight
Output:
fl
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
3
dog
racecar
car
Output:
none
```
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 200`
- Each word is 1 to 200 lowercase English letters.

title: Reverse Words in a String
description:
A line holds words separated by one or more spaces. Print the same words in the opposite order, with exactly one space between neighbours and no spaces at either end.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the sentence. It may begin with spaces and may use runs of several spaces between words.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the words in reverse order, joined by single spaces.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
the sky is blue
Output:
blue is sky the
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
a good   example
Output:
example good a
```
constraints:
- The line is 1 to 300 characters long.
- It contains only English letters, digits, and spaces.
- It holds at least one word.

title: Zigzag Conversion
description:
Write a string downwards and diagonally across a fixed number of rows: fill the rows top to bottom, then climb back up diagonally to the top row, and repeat until the string runs out. Then read the layout back one row at a time, left to right.

For `PAYPALISHIRING` with 3 rows the layout is

```
P   A   H   N
A P L S I I G
Y   I   R
```

so the reading is `PAHNAPLSIIGYIR`.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the string.
- Line 2: the integer number of rows.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the row-by-row reading of the layout.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
PAYPALISHIRING
3
Output:
PAHNAPLSIIGYIR
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
PAYPALISHIRING
4
Output:
PINALSIGYAHRPI
```
constraints:
- The string is 1 to 500 characters long.
- It contains only English letters, commas, and full stops.
- `1 <= number of rows <= 500`

title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
description:
Report where a pattern first appears inside a longer string.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the haystack, the string being searched.
- Line 2: the needle, the pattern to find.

Output (stdout):

- One line with the index of the first character of the first match, counting from 0, or `-1` when the needle never appears.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
sadbutsad
sad
Output:
0
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
leetcode
leeto
Output:
-1
```
constraints: - Each string is 1 to 200 lowercase English letters.

title: Text Justification
description:
Lay out words into lines of exactly `maxWidth` characters. Walk the words in order and put as many as fit on the current line, where a line needs at least one space between neighbouring words. Pad every line but the last so it is exactly `maxWidth` wide: spread the extra spaces over the gaps between words, and when they do not divide evenly give the extra spaces to the leftmost gaps first. A line holding a single word, and the final line, are left aligned and padded on the right.

Input (stdin):

- Line 1: the integer `maxWidth`.
- Line 2: the words, separated by single spaces.

Output (stdout):

- One line per laid out line. Each one is printed between two `|` characters, so that the padding spaces are visible: exactly `maxWidth` characters sit between the bars.
examples:
**Example 1**

```
Input:
16
This is an example of text justification.
Output:
|This    is    an|
|example  of text|
|justification.  |
```

**Example 2**

```
Input:
10
a b c d e f g
Output:
|a  b c d e|
|f g       |
```
constraints:
- `1 <= maxWidth <= 100`
- There are 1 to 300 words.
- Each word is 1 to `maxWidth` characters of printable non-space text.

testCases.input:
16
This is an example of text justification.

16
What must be acknowledgment shall be

20
Science is what we understand well enough to explain to a computer. Art is everything else we do
testCases.output:
|Science  is  what we|
|understand      well|
|enough to explain to|
|a  computer.  Art is|
|everything  else  we|
|do                  |

testCases.input:
10
a b c d e f g

title: Valid Palindrome
description:
A phrase counts as a palindrome when, after dropping every character that is not a letter or a digit and lowering the case of the letters that remain, the text reads the same from the front and from the back. Decide whether the given phrase is a palindrome.

**Input**

A single line holding the phrase. The whole line is the phrase, inner spaces included, so do not split it on whitespace. The phrase never starts or ends with a space.

**Output**

Print `true` when the phrase is a palindrome and `false` otherwise, in lower case. A phrase with no letters or digits at all counts as a palindrome.
examples:
```
Input
A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

Output
true
```

```
Input
race a car

Output
false
```
constraints:
- The phrase holds between 1 and 200000 characters.
- Every character is printable ASCII.
- The phrase has no leading or trailing spaces.

testCases.input: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
Was it a car or a cat I saw?

title: Is Subsequence
description:
One string is a subsequence of another when you can delete some characters of the longer string, without reordering what is left, and end up with the shorter one. Decide whether the first string is a subsequence of the second.

**Input**

Line 1: the candidate string.

Line 2: the host string.

**Output**

Print `true` when the candidate is a subsequence of the host and `false` otherwise, in lower case.
examples:
```
Input
abc
ahbgdc

Output
true
```

```
Input
axc
ahbgdc

Output
false
```
constraints:
- Each string holds between 1 and 100000 lower case English letters.
- Neither line is blank.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
description:
Given a list of integers already sorted from smallest to largest, find two different positions whose values add up to a target.

**Input**

Line 1: two integers, the count of values and the target.

Line 2: that many integers in non-decreasing order, separated by spaces.

**Output**

Print the two positions as one-based indices, smaller index first, separated by a single space. When more than one pair works, print the pair with the smallest first index, and among those the one with the smallest second index. Print `-1` when no pair adds up to the target.
constraints:
- The count of values is between 2 and 30000.
- Each value and the target lie between -1000 and 1000.
- The values are given in non-decreasing order.

title: Container With Most Water
description:
Each value in the list is the height of a vertical line standing at that position, one unit apart. Pick two lines so that the rectangle they form with the horizontal axis holds the most water. The water level is capped by the shorter of the two lines, and the width is the distance between their positions.

**Input**

Line 1: one integer, the number of lines.

Line 2: that many non-negative integers, the heights, separated by spaces.

**Output**

Print the largest area as a single integer.
constraints:
- The number of lines is between 2 and 100000.
- Each height lies between 0 and 10000.

title: 3Sum
description:
Find every group of three values in the list that adds up to zero. Two groups count as the same when they use the same multiset of values, so each distinct combination of values is reported once even if the list repeats it.

**Input**

Line 1: one integer, the number of values.

Line 2: that many integers separated by spaces.

**Output**

Print one triplet per line. Inside a triplet the three values are sorted from smallest to largest and separated by single spaces. The lines themselves are sorted lexicographically, that is by first value, then second, then third. Print `none` when no triplet adds up to zero.
constraints:
- The number of values is between 1 and 3000.
- Each value lies between -100000 and 100000.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
description:
Find the shortest run of neighbouring values whose sum is at least the target. A run must be contiguous, and its length is the count of values it covers.

**Input**

Line 1: two integers, the count of values and the target.

Line 2: that many positive integers separated by spaces.

**Output**

Print the length of the shortest qualifying run as a single integer. Print `0` when no run reaches the target.
constraints:
- The count of values is between 1 and 100000.
- Each value lies between 1 and 10000.
- The target lies between 1 and 1000000000.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description:
Find the longest stretch of neighbouring characters in the string in which no character appears twice. Only the length is asked for, not the stretch itself.

**Input**

A single line holding the string. It contains no spaces.

**Output**

Print the length of the longest repeat-free stretch as a single integer.
examples:
```
Input
abcabcbb

Output
3
```

```
Input
pwwkew

Output
3
```
constraints:
- The string holds between 1 and 50000 characters.
- Every character is a printable ASCII character other than a space.

title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
description:
Every word in the word list has the same length. A window of the text is a match when it is exactly the words of the list glued together in some order, each word used as many times as it appears in the list. Find where every such window starts.

**Input**

Line 1: the text, a string with no spaces.

Line 2: the words, separated by single spaces.

**Output**

Print the zero-based starting positions of the matching windows in ascending order, separated by single spaces, on one line. Print `none` when no window matches.
examples:
```
Input
barfoothefoobarman
foo bar

Output
0 9
```

```
Input
wordgoodgoodgoodbestword
word good best word

Output
none
```
constraints:
- The text holds between 1 and 10000 lower case English letters.
- There are between 1 and 5000 words.
- Every word holds between 1 and 30 lower case English letters.
- All words have the same length.

title: Minimum Window Substring
description:
Find the shortest stretch of neighbouring characters in the text that contains every character of the pattern, counting repeats: a character needed three times must appear at least three times inside the stretch. Extra characters are allowed.

**Input**

Line 1: the text, a string with no spaces.

Line 2: the pattern, a string with no spaces.

**Output**

Print the shortest covering stretch exactly as it appears in the text. When several stretches tie on length, print the one that starts furthest to the left. Print `none` when no stretch covers the pattern.
examples:
```
Input
ADOBECODEBANC
ABC

Output
BANC
```

```
Input
a
aa

Output
none
```
constraints:
- The text and the pattern each hold between 1 and 100000 characters.
- Every character is an English letter, upper or lower case.

title: Valid Sudoku
description:
A partially filled 9 by 9 Sudoku board is valid when no digit repeats inside any single row, inside any single column, or inside any of the nine 3 by 3 blocks. Empty cells are ignored, and the board does not have to be solvable.

**Input**

Nine lines, each holding nine cells separated by single spaces. A cell is either a digit from `1` to `9` or a dot `.` for an empty cell.

**Output**

Print `true` when the board breaks no rule and `false` otherwise, in lower case.
constraints:
- The board is always exactly 9 rows of 9 cells.
- Every cell is a digit from 1 to 9 or a dot.

title: Spiral Matrix
description:
Walk the matrix in a clockwise spiral: start at the top-left cell, run along the top row to the right, down the right column, back along the bottom row to the left, up the left column, then repeat on the ring that is left over. Report the values in the order they are visited.

**Input**

Line 1: two integers, the number of rows and the number of columns.

Line 2 onwards: that many rows, each holding the row's cells as integers separated by single spaces.

**Output**

Print every value in spiral order on one line, separated by single spaces.
constraints:
- The number of rows and columns are each between 1 and 10.
- Each cell lies between -100 and 100.

title: Rotate Image
description:
Turn a square matrix a quarter turn clockwise, so the first row becomes the last column, the second row becomes the second to last column, and so on.

**Input**

Line 1: one integer, the side length of the matrix.

Line 2 onwards: that many rows, each holding that many integers separated by single spaces.

**Output**

Print the rotated matrix, one row per line, the values of a row separated by single spaces.
constraints:
- The side length is between 1 and 20.
- Each cell lies between -1000 and 1000.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description:
Wherever the matrix holds a zero, the whole row and the whole column through that cell become zero. All zeroes present in the original matrix trigger this at once, so zeroes written by the process do not spread further.

**Input**

Line 1: two integers, the number of rows and the number of columns.

Line 2 onwards: that many rows, each holding the row's cells as integers separated by single spaces.

**Output**

Print the updated matrix, one row per line, the values of a row separated by single spaces.
constraints:
- The number of rows and columns are each between 1 and 200.
- Each cell lies between -2147483648 and 2147483647.

title: Game of Life
description:
Each cell of the board is live, written `1`, or dead, written `0`. A cell has up to eight neighbours, counting diagonals, and cells outside the board do not exist. Every cell updates at the same time from the current board: a live cell with two or three live neighbours stays live and dies otherwise, and a dead cell with exactly three live neighbours becomes live. Report the board after one such update.

**Input**

Line 1: two integers, the number of rows and the number of columns.

Line 2 onwards: that many rows, each holding the row's cells as `0` or `1` separated by single spaces.

**Output**

Print the next board, one row per line, the values of a row separated by single spaces.
constraints:
- The number of rows and columns are each between 1 and 25.
- Every cell is 0 or 1.

title: Ransom Note
description:
Letters are cut out of a magazine to spell a ransom note. Each letter of the
magazine may be used at most once. Decide whether the note can be built.

Input is two lines:

1. the ransom note, a non-empty string of lowercase letters
2. the magazine, a non-empty string of lowercase letters

Print `true` if the note can be built from the magazine letters, otherwise print
`false`.
examples:
**Example 1**

Input

```
aa
ab
```

Output

```
false
```

**Example 2**

Input

```
aa
aab
```

Output

```
true
```
constraints:
- 1 <= length of the note <= 100000
- 1 <= length of the magazine <= 100000
- both lines contain only lowercase English letters

title: Isomorphic Strings
description:
Two strings of equal length are isomorphic when one can be turned into the other
by replacing letters, where every occurrence of a letter is replaced by the same
letter and no two letters are replaced by the same letter.

Input is two lines:

1. the first string, lowercase letters
2. the second string, lowercase letters, the same length as the first

Print `true` when the strings are isomorphic, otherwise print `false`.
examples:
**Example 1**

Input

```
egg
add
```

Output

```
true
```

**Example 2**

Input

```
foo
bar
```

Output

```
false
```

Evaluate an arithmetic expression written in postfix form, where each operator

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
topics: Tree, Depth-First Search, Breadth-First Search, Binary Tree
description:
The depth of a binary tree is the number of nodes you pass through on the longest walk from the root down to a leaf. Read one tree and report that number.

The tree arrives as a single line of level-order tokens. Each token is either an integer or the word `null`, which marks a missing child. The tokens are read breadth first: the first token is the root, the next two are the root's children, the next four are those nodes' children, and so on, where a `null` contributes no children of its own. Trailing `null` tokens are left out. For instance `3 9 20 null null 15 7` is a root `3` with children `9` and `20`, where `9` is a leaf and `20` has children `15` and `7`.

Print a single line holding the depth as a decimal integer.

```
3
```

```
5
```

The tokens are read breadth first: the first token is the root, the next two are the root's children, the next four are those nodes' children, and so on, where a `null` contributes no children of its own. Trailing `null` tokens are left out. For instance `3 9 20 null null 15 7` is a root `3` with children `9` and `20`, where `9` is a leaf and `20` has children `15` and `7`.

The input is two such lines: the first tree on line one, the second tree on line two.

Print a single line holding `true` or `false`, in lower case.

Print the resulting tree on one line using the very same level-order encoding: values and `null` tokens separated by single spaces, with trailing `null` tokens dropped.

- The printed line drops trailing `null` tokens.

A binary tree is symmetric when its left half is the mirror image of its right half, both in shape and in values. Read one tree and say whether it is symmetric.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
topics: Tree, Breadth-First Search, Depth-First Search, Binary Tree
description:

title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
topics: Divide and Conquer, Binary Search Tree, Tree, Array
description:
Turn a sorted array of distinct integers into a height-balanced binary search tree. Many balanced trees fit the same array, so the shape is pinned down by one rule: for the index range low to high, the root of that range is always the element at index `(low + high) // 2`. When the range holds an even number of elements, that rule picks the left of the two middle elements. Elements before the chosen index build the left subtree and elements after it build the right subtree, by the same rule.

**Input**

The first line holds n, the number of elements. The second line holds the n elements in increasing order, separated by spaces.

**Output**

One line holding the resulting tree in level-order (breadth-first) encoding: the root value first, then two tokens for every node already placed, its left child then its right child, with `null` for a missing child and trailing `null` tokens omitted.

```
Input
7
-10 -3 0 5 9 12 20
Output
5 -3 12 -10 0 9 20
```

Indices 0 to 6 pick index 3, the value 5, as the root.

**Example 2**

```
Input
4
1 2 3 4
Output
2 1 3 null null null 4
```

Indices 0 to 3 pick index 1, so the root is 2 rather than 3.
constraints:
- 1 <= n <= 10000.
- Elements are distinct and given in strictly increasing order.
- Each element fits in the range -10^4 to 10^4.

title: Clone Graph
topics: Graph, Hash Table, Depth-First Search, Breadth-First Search
description:
You are given a connected or disconnected undirected graph whose nodes are labelled `1` to `n`. Build a deep copy of it: a fresh node object per original node, wired to the copies of its neighbours. **Input**

- The first line holds `n`, the number of nodes.
- Each of the next `n` lines describes one node, in label order starting at `1`: the node's neighbour count, then that many neighbour labels separated by single spaces. A node with no neighbours is the single value `0`.

**Output**

- `n` lines, one per node in label order. Each line holds the label, a colon, a space, then the labels of that node's neighbours **in the copied graph** in ascending order, separated by single spaces. When a node has no neighbours, print the word `none` in their place.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 100`
- Every neighbour label is between `1` and `n`.
- There are no self loops and no repeated edges.
- Edges are undirected, so each edge appears in both of its endpoints' lines.

title: Course Schedule

description:
A degree has `numCourses` courses, numbered `0` to `numCourses - 1`. A prerequisite pair `a b` means course `b` has to be finished before course `a` can be taken. Decide whether all the courses can be finished.

**Input**

- The first line holds two integers: `numCourses` and the number of prerequisite pairs.
- Each of the next lines holds one pair `a b`, meaning `b` comes before `a`.

**Output**

- A single line holding `true` when every course can be finished, otherwise `false`.

```
true
```

**Example 2**

```

false
```

title: Course Schedule II
topics: Graph, Topological Sort, Heap (Priority Queue), Breadth-First Search
description:
A degree has `numCourses` courses, numbered `0` to `numCourses - 1`. A prerequisite pair `a b` means course `b` has to be finished before course `a` can be taken. Produce an order in which all the courses can be taken.

Many orders are usually valid, so exactly one is accepted: the **lexicographically smallest** one. Read the order as a sequence of course numbers and compare sequences position by position; the accepted answer is the smallest under that comparison. In practice this means that whenever several courses have all their prerequisites met, the one with the smallest number is taken next.

**Input**

- The first line holds two integers: `numCourses` and the number of prerequisite pairs.
- Each of the next lines holds one pair `a b`, meaning `b` comes before `a`.

**Output**

- A single line holding the course numbers in order, separated by single spaces. When no order exists, print the word `none` instead.
constraints:
- `1 <= numCourses <= 2000`
- `0 <= pairs <= 5000`
- `0 <= a, b < numCourses` and `a != b`
- No pair is repeated.

title: Snakes and Ladders
topics: Array, Matrix, Breadth-First Search, Shortest Path
description:
An `n` by `n` board is numbered from `1` to `n * n` in boustrophedon order: numbering starts in the bottom left corner, runs right along the bottom row, then turns and runs left along the row above it, alternating direction on every row.

A turn works like this. From square `s` you may move to any of `s + 1` through `s + 6`, as long as the number does not pass `n * n`. If the square you land on carries a snake or ladder, you are moved to its destination immediately. You never take a second snake or ladder in the same turn, even when the destination carries one. Find the fewest turns needed to land exactly on square `n * n`.

**Input**

- The first line holds `n`.
- Each of the next `n` lines holds `n` integers separated by single spaces, given top row first. A value of `-1` means the square is plain; any other value is the destination square of the snake or ladder on that square.

**Output**

- A single line with the fewest turns, or `-1` when the last square cannot be reached.
constraints:
- `2 <= n <= 20`, plus the degenerate `n = 1` board, where the answer is `0`.
- Each value is `-1` or a square number between `1` and `n * n`.
- A snake or ladder never starts on square `1` or on square `n * n`.

A mutation is only allowed when the gene it produces appears in the gene bank. Starting from the start gene, count the fewest mutations that turn it into the end gene.

The start gene itself does not have to be in the bank. When the start gene already equals the end gene the answer is `0`, whatever the bank holds.

**Input**

- The first line holds the start gene.
- The second line holds the end gene.
- The third line holds the number of genes in the bank.
- Each of the next lines holds one bank gene.

**Output**

- A single line with the fewest mutations, or `-1` when the end gene cannot be reached.

```

AACCGCTA

Output
-1
```
constraints:
- Every gene is 8 characters long and uses only `A`, `C`, `G` and `T`.
- `0 <= bank size <= 10`
- The bank may be empty, in which case only the start equals end case answers anything but `-1`.

title: Combinations
description:
Given two integers `n` and `k`, list every way of choosing `k` different numbers out of `1` to `n`. The order within a choice does not matter, so each choice is listed once.

**Input**

- A single line holding `n` and `k`, separated by a space.

- One choice per line, its numbers in ascending order and separated by single spaces.
- The lines are sorted by comparing the choices as number sequences, position by position, smallest first. Compare numbers as numbers, not as text, so `2` comes before `10`.

title: Permutations

**Input**

- The first line holds `m`, how many numbers follow.
- The second line holds the `m` numbers, separated by single spaces.

**Output**

- One arrangement per line, its numbers separated by single spaces.
- The lines are sorted by comparing the arrangements as number sequences, position by position, smallest first. Compare numbers as numbers, not as text, so `2` comes before `10` and `-1` comes before both.
constraints:
- `1 <= m <= 6`
- `-10 <= each number <= 10`, and all the numbers are distinct.

title: Combination Sum
description:
Given a list of distinct positive integers and a target, list every group of them that adds up exactly to the target. A number may be used as many times as you like, and two groups count as the same group when they use the same numbers the same number of times.

**Input**

- The first line holds two integers: how many candidate numbers follow, and the target.
- The second line holds the candidate numbers, separated by single spaces.

**Output**

- One group per line, its numbers in ascending order and separated by single spaces.
- The lines are sorted by comparing the groups as number sequences, position by position, smallest first; when one group is a prefix of another, the shorter one comes first.
- When nothing adds up to the target, print the word `none` instead.
constraints:
- `1 <= candidates <= 8`, all distinct.
- `2 <= each candidate <= 40`
- `1 <= target <= 40`

**Input**

- A single line holding `n`.

**Output**

- A single line with the number of arrangements. It is `0` when no arrangement exists.

title: Generate Parentheses

Given a number of bracket pairs, list every well formed string built from them. A string is well formed when every opening bracket is closed later and no closing bracket ever comes before the opening bracket it belongs to.

**Input**

**Output**

- One string per line, each of length `2 * n`, and the whole list sorted lexicographically, meaning ordinary string order where `(` sorts before `)`.
- When `n` is `0` there is nothing to list, so print the word `none` instead.

title: Maximum Subarray
topics: Array, Divide and Conquer, Dynamic Programming
description:
Given a list of integers, find the contiguous block of one or more
neighbouring values whose sum is as large as possible, and report that sum.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` integers separated by single spaces.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the largest sum of any contiguous non-empty block.

- `1 <= n <= 10^5`
- `-10^4 <= values[i] <= 10^4`
- The chosen block must contain at least one value.

title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
topics: Array, Divide and Conquer, Dynamic Programming, Queue
description:
The values form a ring, so the element after the last one is the first
one again. Find the largest sum of a run of one or more neighbouring values on that
ring, where a run may wrap past the end but may not use any element twice.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` integers separated by single spaces.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the largest such sum.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 10^4`
- `-3 * 10^4 <= values[i] <= 3 * 10^4`
- A run holds between 1 and `n` elements.

title: Search Insert Position
description:
A list of distinct integers is already sorted from smallest to largest.
Report the index of a target value, or, when the target is missing, the index it would
occupy if it were inserted while keeping the list sorted. Indices start at zero.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` sorted integers separated by single spaces.
- Line 3: the target integer.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding that index.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 10^4`
- `-10^4 <= values[i] <= 10^4`
- The values are strictly increasing.
- `-10^4 <= target <= 10^4`

title: Search a 2D Matrix
description:
A grid of integers is sorted twice over: each row increases from left to
right, and the first value of every row is larger than the last value of the row above
it. Report whether a target value appears anywhere in the grid.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: two integers `rows` and `cols` separated by a space.
- Next `rows` lines: `cols` integers each, separated by single spaces.
- Last line: the target integer.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding `true` when the target is present, otherwise `false`.
constraints:
- `1 <= rows, cols <= 100`
- `-10^4 <= grid value <= 10^4`
- Reading the grid row by row gives one strictly increasing sequence.
- `-10^4 <= target <= 10^4`

title: Find Peak Element

An index is a peak when its value is larger than the value on each side of
it. Positions off either end of the list count as smaller than everything, so the first
and last index only have to beat their single neighbour. Several peaks can exist, so
report the smallest index that is a peak.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` integers separated by single spaces.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the smallest peak index, counting from zero.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 10^5`
- `-2^31 <= values[i] <= 2^31 - 1`
- No two neighbouring values are equal, so at least one peak always exists.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description:
A sorted list of distinct integers was cut at one position and the two
pieces were swapped, so the values rise, drop once, then rise again. Report the index of
a target value in this rotated list, or `-1` when it is not there.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` integers separated by single spaces.
- Line 3: the target integer.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the index of the target, counting from zero, or `-1`.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 5000`
- `-10^4 <= values[i] <= 10^4`
- All values are distinct.
- The list is a rotation of a sorted list, possibly by zero positions.

title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
description:
A list of integers is sorted from smallest to largest and may repeat
values. Report the first and the last index at which a target value appears. When the
target is missing, report `-1 -1`.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` sorted integers separated by single spaces.
- Line 3: the target integer.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the first index and the last index, separated by one space.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 10^5`
- `-10^9 <= values[i] <= 10^9`

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

A sorted list of distinct integers was cut at one position and the two
pieces were swapped. Report the smallest value in the resulting list.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` integers separated by single spaces.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the smallest value.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 5000`
- `-5000 <= values[i] <= 5000`
- All values are distinct.
- The list is a rotation of a sorted list, possibly by zero positions.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
topics: Array, Binary Search, Divide and Conquer

Two sorted lists of integers are given. Imagine every value from both
lists placed in one sorted sequence, and report its median: the middle value when the
combined count is odd, or the average of the two middle values when it is even.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `m`, the size of the first list.
- Line 2: `m` sorted integers separated by single spaces.
- Line 3: an integer `n`, the size of the second list.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the median written with exactly five digits after the decimal

- `-10^6 <= value <= 10^6`

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array

by distinctness, so in `[3, 2, 3, 1]` the second largest is `3`.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` integers separated by single spaces.
- Line 3: an integer `k`.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the kth largest value.

title: IPO

You start with `w` units of capital and may finish at most `k` of `n`
projects, one after another. Project `i` can only be started once your capital is at
least `capital[i]`, and finishing it adds `profit[i]` to your capital forever. Report the
largest capital you can hold at the end. Stop early when no remaining project is
affordable.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `k`, the most projects you may finish.
- Line 2: an integer `w`, your starting capital.
- Line 3: an integer `n`, how many projects exist.
- Line 4: `n` integers, the profit of each project, separated by single spaces.
- Line 5: `n` integers, the capital each project requires, in the same project order.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the final capital.

title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums

Two sorted lists are given. A pair takes one value `u` from the first list
and one value `v` from the second, and every combination of positions counts as its own
pair even when the values repeat. Print the `k` pairs with the smallest sums.

Order the printed pairs by sum from smallest to largest; break a tie in sum by the
smaller `u`, and a remaining tie by the smaller `v`. When `k` is larger than the number
of pairs that exist, print every pair.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `m`, the size of the first list.
- Line 2: `m` sorted integers separated by single spaces.
- Line 3: an integer `n`, the size of the second list.
- Line 4: `n` sorted integers separated by single spaces.
- Line 5: an integer `k`.

Output (to standard output):
- One line per printed pair, holding `u` and `v` separated by a single space.
constraints:
- `1 <= m, n <= 1000`
- `-10^9 <= value <= 10^9`
- Each list never decreases from left to right.
- `1 <= k <= 1000`

title: Find Median from Data Stream
topics: Design, Two Pointers, Data Stream, Sorting, Heap
description:
Numbers arrive one at a time, and at any moment you may be asked for the
median of everything seen so far. The median is the middle value when the count is odd,
or the average of the two middle values when it is even.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `q`, how many operations follow.
- Next `q` lines: either `addNum x`, which records the integer `x`, or `findMedian`,
  which asks for the median of the values recorded so far.

Output (to standard output):
- One line per `findMedian` operation, in the order the operations appear, holding the
  median written with exactly five digits after the decimal point.
examples:
```
Input:
5
addNum 1
addNum 2
findMedian
addNum 3
findMedian
Output:
1.50000
2.00000
```

```
Input:
4
addNum -1
addNum -2
addNum -3
findMedian
Output:
-2.00000
```
constraints:
- `2 <= q <= 10^4`
- `-10^5 <= x <= 10^5`
- The first operation is always `addNum`, so `findMedian` never runs on an empty set.
- At least one operation is `findMedian`.

findMedian

findMedian

title: Add Binary
description:
Two non-negative numbers are written in base two. Add them and print the
sum, also in base two.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: the first binary string.
- Line 2: the second binary string.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the sum in base two, with no leading zeros unless the sum is
  zero, which prints as `0`.
constraints:
- Each string has between 1 and 10^4 characters.
- Each character is `0` or `1`.
- Neither input string has a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

title: Reverse Bits
description:
Treat the given value as an unsigned 32-bit integer, so it is written with
exactly 32 bits and is never negative. Reverse the order of those 32 bits, so the lowest
bit becomes the highest and the highest becomes the lowest, then print the value the
reversed bits spell out.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: a single integer between `0` and `4294967295`.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the reversed value in ordinary decimal notation.
constraints:
- `0 <= value <= 4294967295`, that is, `2^32 - 1`.
- The value is unsigned, so bit 31 carries no sign.

title: Number of 1 Bits
description:
Treat the given value as an unsigned 32-bit integer and count how many of
its bits are set to one.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: a single integer between `0` and `4294967295`.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the count of one bits.
constraints:
- `0 <= value <= 4294967295`, that is, `2^32 - 1`.
- The value is unsigned, so bit 31 carries no sign.

title: Single Number
description:
Every value in the list appears exactly twice except for one, which appears
once. Report that lone value.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` integers separated by single spaces.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the value that appears only once.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 3 * 10^4`
- `n` is odd.
- `-3 * 10^4 <= values[i] <= 3 * 10^4`
- Exactly one value appears once; every other value appears exactly twice.

title: Single Number II
description:
Every value in the list appears exactly three times except for one, which
appears once. Report that lone value.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: an integer `n`, how many values follow.
- Line 2: `n` integers separated by single spaces.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the value that appears only once.
constraints:
- `1 <= n <= 3 * 10^4`
- `-2^31 <= values[i] <= 2^31 - 1`
- Exactly one value appears once; every other value appears exactly three times.

title: Bitwise AND of Numbers Range
description:
Take every integer from `left` to `right`, both ends included, and combine
them all with the bitwise AND operator. Print the result.

Input (from standard input):
- Line 1: the integer `left`.
- Line 2: the integer `right`.

Output (to standard output):
- A single line holding the bitwise AND of the whole range.
constraints:
- `0 <= left <= right <= 2^31 - 1`
- `right - left <= 10^5`, so even a plain loop over the range finishes in time.

title: Palindrome Number
description:
Read one integer and decide whether its decimal form reads the same from
left to right as it does from right to left. A leading minus sign counts as part
of the number, so any negative value fails straight away.

Input: a single line holding the integer.

Output: a single line holding `true` when the number is a palindrome and
`false` otherwise.
examples:
```
Input
121

Output
true
```

```
Input
-121

Output
false
```
constraints:
- The integer fits in a signed 32-bit range: -2147483648 to 2147483647.
- The line carries no spaces and no leading zeroes.

title: Plus One
description:
A non-negative whole number is given one digit at a time, most significant digit
first. Add one to that number and print the digits of the result. A number such
as 999 grows an extra digit, so the answer may be one digit longer than the
input.

Input: the first line holds the number of digits. The second line holds that
many digits separated by single spaces.

Output: a single line holding the digits of the incremented number, separated by
single spaces.
constraints:
- 1 <= number of digits <= 100.
- Each digit is between 0 and 9.
- The number has no leading zero unless it is the single digit 0.

title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
description:
Given n, report how many zeroes sit at the end of n factorial. Only count the
unbroken run of zeroes at the very end of the number, not zeroes that appear
elsewhere in it.

Input: a single line holding n.

Output: a single line holding the number of trailing zeroes.

title: Sqrt(x)
description:
Compute the square root of a non-negative integer and throw away anything after
the decimal point. The answer is the largest whole number whose square is still
at most x, so the root of 8 truncates to 2 rather than rounding up to 3.

Input: a single line holding x.

Output: a single line holding the truncated integer square root of x.

title: Pow(x, n)
description:
Raise a decimal number x to an integer power n. The exponent may be negative,
in which case the answer is one divided by x raised to the matching positive
power.

Input: the first line holds x written as a decimal number. The second line holds
the integer exponent n.

Output: a single line holding the result written with exactly five digits after
the decimal point.
constraints:
- -100.0 < x < 100.0 and x is not zero when n is negative.
- -100 <= n <= 100.
- The result always fits in a double precision float.

title: Max Points on a Line
description:
A set of distinct points on a plane is given. Find the largest number of those
points that a single straight line can pass through. A line may run in any
direction, including straight up and down.

Input: the first line holds the number of points. Each of the next lines holds
one point as its x coordinate and its y coordinate separated by a space.

Output: a single line holding the size of the largest group of points lying on
one line.
constraints:
- 1 <= number of points <= 300.
- -10000 <= x, y <= 10000.
- No two given points are the same.

title: Climbing Stairs
description:
A staircase has n steps. Each move climbs either one step or two steps. Count
how many different orders of moves reach the top.

Input: a single line holding n.

Output: a single line holding the number of distinct ways to reach the top.

title: House Robber
description:
Houses stand in a row and each one holds a known amount of money. Two houses
next to each other cannot both be emptied. Work out the largest total that can
be taken.

Input: the first line holds the number of houses. The second line holds that
many house values separated by single spaces.

Output: a single line holding the largest total that can be taken.
constraints:
- 1 <= number of houses <= 15.
- 0 <= house value <= 400.

title: Word Break
description:
Given a string and a dictionary, decide whether the string can be cut into a
sequence of dictionary words laid end to end with nothing left over. A
dictionary word may be reused as many times as needed.

Input: the first line holds the string. The second line holds the number of
dictionary words. Each of the next lines holds one dictionary word.

Output: a single line holding `true` when such a split exists and `false`
otherwise.
examples:
```
Input
leetcode
2
leet
code

Output
true
```

```
Input
catsandog
5
cats
dog
sand
and
cat

Output
false
```
constraints:
- 1 <= length of the string <= 300.
- 1 <= number of dictionary words <= 1000.
- 1 <= length of each dictionary word <= 20.
- Every string holds lowercase English letters only.

title: Coin Change
description:
Coins of given face values are available in unlimited supply. Make up an exact
target amount using as few coins as possible.

Input: the first line holds the target amount. The second line holds the number
of coin types. The third line holds that many coin values separated by single
spaces.

Output: a single line holding the smallest number of coins that reaches the
amount, or `-1` when no combination of the given coins adds up to it.
constraints:
- 0 <= amount <= 10000.
- 1 <= number of coin types <= 12.
- 1 <= coin value <= 1000.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description:
Pick values out of an array, keeping their original left-to-right order, so that
each picked value is strictly larger than the one before it. Report how many
values the longest such pick contains. The picked values need not sit next to
each other in the array.

Input: the first line holds the number of values. The second line holds that
many values separated by single spaces.

Output: a single line holding the length of the longest strictly increasing
pick.
constraints:
- 1 <= number of values <= 9.
- -10000 <= each value <= 10000.

title: Triangle
description:
Numbers are arranged in a triangle whose first row holds one value, second row
two values, and so on. A walk starts at the single top value and, on each step
down, moves to one of the two values directly beneath the current one. Find the
smallest total a walk from the top row to the bottom row can collect.

Input: the first line holds the number of rows. Each of the next lines holds one
row, with row number i carrying i values separated by single spaces.

Output: a single line holding the smallest achievable total.
constraints:
- 1 <= number of rows <= 10.
- -10000 <= each value <= 10000.

title: Minimum Path Sum
description:
A grid of non-negative costs is given. A walk starts at the top-left cell, ends
at the bottom-right cell, and may only step one cell right or one cell down.
Find the smallest total cost such a walk can collect, counting both the starting
cell and the finishing cell.

Input: the first line holds the number of rows and the number of columns,
separated by a space. Each of the next lines holds one grid row with that many
values separated by single spaces.

Output: a single line holding the smallest achievable total cost.
constraints:
- 1 <= rows, columns <= 10.
- 0 <= each grid value <= 200.

title: Unique Paths II
description:
A grid is marked with `0` for an open cell and `1` for a blocked cell. Count the
routes from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell that only step right or
down and never enter a blocked cell. If either the starting cell or the
finishing cell is blocked the answer is 0.

Input: the first line holds the number of rows and the number of columns,
separated by a space. Each of the next lines holds one grid row with that many
markers separated by single spaces.

Output: a single line holding the number of routes.
constraints:
- 1 <= rows, columns <= 10.
- Each marker is 0 or 1.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
description:
Find the longest run of neighbouring characters in a string that reads the same
in both directions. When several runs tie for the longest, print the one that
starts earliest in the string.

Input: a single line holding the string.

Output: a single line holding the leftmost longest palindromic run.
examples:
```
Input
babad

Output
bab
```

```
Input
cbbd

Output
bb
```
constraints:
- 1 <= length of the string <= 1000.
- The string holds lowercase and uppercase English letters only.

title: Interleaving String
description:
Three strings are given. Decide whether the third one can be built by taking the
characters of the first two in order and weaving them together, so that the
characters of each source string keep their relative order and every character
of both source strings is used exactly once.

Input: the first line holds s1, the second line holds s2 and the third line
holds s3.

Output: a single line holding `true` when s3 is such a weave of s1 and s2, and
`false` otherwise.
examples:
```
Input
aabcc
dbbca
aadbbcbcac

Output
true
```

```
Input
aabcc
dbbca
aadbbbaccc

Output
false
```
constraints:
- 1 <= length of s1, s2 <= 50.
- 1 <= length of s3 <= 100.
- Every string holds lowercase English letters only.

title: Edit Distance
description:
Turn one word into another using as few single-character edits as possible. An
edit inserts a character, deletes a character, or replaces one character with
another. Report the smallest number of edits needed.

Input: the first line holds the starting word. The second line holds the target
word.

Output: a single line holding the smallest number of edits.
examples:
```
Input
horse
ros

Output
3
```

```
Input
kitten
sitting

Output
3
```
constraints:
- 1 <= length of each word <= 8.
- Both words hold lowercase English letters only.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
description:
Daily prices of one share are given. At most two complete rounds of buying and
then selling are allowed, and a share must be sold before the next one is
bought. Find the largest profit available. Doing nothing is allowed, so the
answer is never below zero.

Input: the first line holds the number of days. The second line holds that many
prices separated by single spaces, in day order.

Output: a single line holding the largest achievable profit.
constraints:
- 1 <= number of days <= 10.
- 0 <= each price <= 100000.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
description:
Daily prices of one share are given together with a cap k on how many complete
rounds of buying and then selling may be made. A share must be sold before the
next one is bought. Find the largest profit available. Doing nothing is allowed,
so the answer is never below zero.

Input: the first line holds the cap k. The second line holds the number of days.
The third line holds that many prices separated by single spaces, in day order.

Output: a single line holding the largest achievable profit.
constraints:
- 0 <= k <= 10.
- 1 <= number of days <= 10.
- 0 <= each price <= 1000.

title: Maximal Square
description:
A grid is filled with `0` and `1` markers. Find the largest square block made up
only of `1` markers and report its area, which is its side length multiplied by
itself. When the grid holds no `1` marker at all the area is 0.

Input: the first line holds the number of rows and the number of columns,
separated by a space. Each of the next lines holds one grid row with that many
markers separated by single spaces.

Output: a single line holding the area of the largest all-ones square.
constraints:
- 1 <= rows, columns <= 20.
- Each marker is 0 or 1.
